title: Coordinate production processes within the workflow of the nursery by organising the availability of raw material, workers, equipment and space to achieve targets within the quickest time, highest quality and least wastage

lessons.title: Understanding nursery workflow
lessons.html:
How work flows through the nursery

Workflow is the order in which work moves from one step to the next. In a nursery, plants and materials move from the store to the potting shed, into propagation, onto growing blocks and finally to dispatch. When each step has what it needs at the right time, the flow is smooth. When something is missing, work piles up in one place and stops in another.

The four resources to coordinate

  • Raw material: seed, cuttings, plugs, growing media, containers, fertiliser, labels and stakes.
  • Workers: the right number of people with the right skills.
  • Equipment: potting machines, mixers, trolleys, sprayers, tools and irrigation.
  • Space: room in the potting shed, propagation house, tunnels and blocks.

The three goals

Coordination aims for the quickest time, the highest quality and the least wastage at the same time. These goals can pull against each other. Rushing a potting job may finish it quickly but cause poor planting and plant losses. A good supervisor balances speed and quality, and reduces waste of materials, time and plants.

Bottlenecks

A bottleneck is the slowest step that holds up the whole flow. Examples:

  • One media mixer cannot keep up with three potting teams.
  • Only one worker is trained to wean tissue-culture plants.
  • The mist house is full, so cuttings cannot be stuck.
  • Only two trolleys are available to move potted plants to the blocks.

Finding and fixing bottlenecks gives the biggest improvement. Watch where work waits, where people stand idle and where materials pile up. That is usually where the bottleneck is.

lessons.title: Organising materials, workers, equipment and space
lessons.html:
Having everything ready at the right time

Raw material

  • Check stock of media, pots, trays and labels against the coming week's plan and order in time; know how long suppliers take to deliver.
  • Use older stock first (first in, first out) so media and fertiliser do not expire or degrade.
  • Store media covered so it stays clean and does not dry out or get waterlogged.
  • Inspect deliveries on arrival and report wrong or damaged goods immediately.

Workers

  • Plan the team for each task using known work rates.
  • Set up tasks as a line where possible: one person fills, one plants, one places on trolleys. A balanced line keeps everyone busy.
  • Have a backup person trained for key tasks.
  • Move workers between tasks when one area is ahead and another is behind.

Equipment

  • Check machines and tools before the shift starts.
  • Arrange servicing at quiet times, not during peak potting.
  • Report faults and take broken equipment out of use until repaired.
  • Only trained workers may operate machines, with guards in place.

Space

  • Plan where each new batch will go before it is produced.
  • Move ready plants on so that space is freed for the next batch.
  • Keep paths clear for trolleys and safe walking.
  • Use space well: well-spaced, labelled blocks are easier to manage and pick.

Coordination tools

Simple tools help: a weekly planning board, a daily task list, a materials checklist, and a space map showing which blocks are full, empty or due to be cleared. Short meetings with other section supervisors, such as dispatch and propagation, prevent clashes over workers, trolleys or space.

lessons.title: Reducing wastage and improving quality
lessons.html:
Doing it right the first time

Types of waste in the nursery

WasteExample
Plant lossesCuttings that do not root, plants that die from drought or disease
Material wasteSpilled media, broken pots, excess fertiliser
Time wasteWorkers waiting for materials, extra walking, rework
Water and energyLeaking pipes, irrigation running in rain, lights left on
Over-productionGrowing more of a plant than can be sold

How to reduce waste

  • Train workers well so tasks are done correctly the first time.
  • Use standard methods, for example the same media mix and potting depth every time.
  • Check quality early in each task so errors are not repeated across thousands of plants.
  • Keep the work area tidy so materials are not lost or contaminated.
  • Fix leaks and check irrigation timers, especially after rain.
  • Record losses and their causes so they can be prevented next time.

Quality at every step

Quality is built into each step, not inspected in at the end. A plant potted crooked or too deep will never become a top-grade plant. Agree on the standard for each step with your team, show examples of good and poor work, and check against the standard during the day.

Measuring performance

Track a few simple measures: units produced per worker per day, percentage of plants lost at each stage, materials used per batch and on-time completion of the plan. Share results with the team and look for steady improvement.

Safety in a fast workflow

Pressure to finish quickly must never lead to unsafe shortcuts. Lift heavy bags and pots correctly or with help, do not overload trolleys, keep guards on machines and wear the required protective equipment.

Key points

  • Coordinate four resources: raw material, workers, equipment and space.
  • Aim for quick time, high quality and least waste together.
  • Find and fix bottlenecks where work waits or piles up.
  • Plan materials and space ahead and use first in, first out.
  • Build quality into each step and record losses and causes.
  • Never take unsafe shortcuts to save time.
